page: Amazon Web Services m1.large is a legacy, first-generation general-purpose server instance. It features an x86_64 architecture powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2651 v2 processor running at a clock speed of 1.8 GHz. The instance provides 2 dedicated physical cores with 1 thread per core, paired with 8.0 GB of system memory, yielding 3.75 GB of RAM per core. It utilizes the Xen hypervisor for virtualization.

A key hardware feature of the m1.large is its bundled local storage, consisting of 840 GB of HDD capacity. This local storage is integrated directly, though it relies on legacy rotational media rather than solid-state technology. Networking is provisioned with a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps. No graphics processing units are included in this configuration.

Across standardized benchmarks, the m1.large exhibits performance metrics in the bottom 10% tier. Stress-ng single-core and multi-core CPU tests, Geekbench scores, and Passmark evaluations consistently rank the instance in the lower performance bracket. Memory bandwidth is similarly limited, with uncached read speeds of 11.1 GB/sec and write speeds of 9.52 GB/sec. The lack of modern CPU instruction sets, such as AVX, AVX512, and AMX, limits its mathematical and vector processing capabilities, though it does support hardware-accelerated AES cryptography.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the m1.large represents a legacy tier with low compute density and low performance-per-resource relative to modern instances. However, the inclusion of 840 GB of local HDD storage provides a high storage-to-compute ratio without requiring external block storage attachments. This instance is best suited for legacy applications, basic file hosting, low-traffic static web serving, or non-critical database testing where storage volume is prioritized over high-speed processing.
